$TWST I want to address Twist's current price. Many bulls sold too early and many bears shorted too early, showing how misunderstood this stock is.

Is the current valuation stretched? Yes.

At a $12B market cap against guided FY26 revenue of $456–457M, Twist trades at about 26x forward sales. Mature life-sciences tools leaders typically trade between 4x and 8x. With 21% top-line growth, a 52% gross margin, an annualized GAAP net loss of about $140M, and Adjusted EBITDA only reaching breakeven by Q4, the stock looks significantly overvalued on near-term fundamentals. The market is pricing in 5-8 years of flawless execution.

So why is the market paying this premium? 🤔

Most assume it's all just AI hype, and that's partially true since AI-driven drug discovery is the most well-known tailwind. As AI models design millions of proteins, Twist acts as the physical, high-volume wet-lab validation engine, directly integrated into AWS, Benchling, and Lilly's TuneLab.

They're able to fill this key role due to their biggest moat, a proprietary semiconductor platform. Writing DNA on silicon chips instead of plastic plates shrinks chemical reaction volumes by 99.8%, permanently lowering the unit cost floor while printing over 1M unique oligos per chip. This automated, high-throughput manufacturing moat can't be easily replicated.

But this is all pretty well-known and has been effectively priced in.

Twist could potentially benefit from some royalties, milestones payments, and downstream stakes in partners' clinical assets and their DNA data storage business spin-off (Atlas) down the road. But this is too speculative to explain the current price...

So I believe the premium is actually anchored in 3 key advantages:

1) Built-In Operating Leverage

Twist operates at less than 50% capacity across their Wilsonville and San Francisco sites, with 65K sqft of unbuilt space ready for expansion. They can scale revenue from about $457M past $1B on existing leases without building new factories. With fixed overhead already absorbed, about 70% of every incremental revenue dollar drops directly to gross profit.

2) Planned Expansion to Clinical cGMP

Currently, Twist operates under a Research Use Only label, losing accounts to legacy CDMOs once drug candidates enter human trials. Their planned expansion into clinical-grade cGMP could be a game changer. Supplying clinical mRNA cancer vaccine templates and cell therapy payloads commands prices 5-50x higher than research tools. This transition could push gross margins past 60–65% and accelerate revenue beyond $1.2B by 2030, compressing forward sales multiples down to 8–10x.

3) Tailwinds Across High-Growth Frontiers

While AI-Driven drug discovery is the most well-known catalyst, there are several more lesser-known tailwinds:

• Minimal Residual Disease (MRD): In cancer recurrence monitoring, Twist's sub-24-hour MRD Express synthesizes up to 1,800 custom probes per patient. As customers like Personalis/Tempus expand testing, Twist captures recurring consumable sales on every serial blood draw across a $20B addressable market.

• Bispecific Antibodies & ADCs: Through their B-Body partnership, Twist offers biopharma a flat-fee, zero-milestone, zero-royalty licensing model that undercuts traditional platform rivals while retaining 80% of license fees and 100% of service work.

• Gene Editing & Cell Therapy: Twist manufactures ultra-long oligos up to 350 nucleotides for prime editing and complex genes up to 7K base pairs for non-viral CAR-T and CRISPR knock-ins.

• Nucleic Acid Therapeutics (mRNA, siRNA, ASO): Twist prints massive oligo tiling pools for siRNA/ASO discovery and complex clonal genes up to 7,000 bp for cell-free mRNA/circRNA templates, eliminating legacy plasmid fermentation delays.

So yes, Twist is expensive by today's numbers so the price could fall short-term. But long-term, they should benefit from economies of scale across several disruptive growth themes.

I'm holding. NFA.

THESIS  
Assisted dying was sold as mercy for people who were already dying. Once the law dropped the dying part, it stopped being the same service. Put the original gate back: terminal illness only.

The claim in one line  
If the state is going to license doctors to end a life, the person should be dying of the disease—not just suffering from life.

Why the original limit existed  
The first statutes and the Oregon-style laws were built for a narrow case: an adult, competent, with a short prognosis, whose death was coming anyway. That was the political bargain. Suffering without a foreseeable death was supposed to be treated, housed, palliated, and supported—not converted into an eligibility category.

What changed  
Courts and later bills removed the “reasonably foreseeable death” test in some countries. Canada’s 2016 law had it. The 2021 rewrite did not. Netherlands and Belgium never used a short-prognosis gate; their text was always “unbearable suffering.” Those are different products wearing the same brand name. Calling both “the original intent” is how the expansion happened without a new public vote on the new product.

The reform, stripped of paperwork  
Restore a terminal-prognosis requirement in every statute that used to have one.  
Do not pretend a chronic, non-fatal condition is the same legal object as end-stage cancer.  
Keep capacity, voluntariness, and independent assessment. Those are safeguards. The missing piece is the dying part.  
Fund the things that make “unbearable” less often a synonym for “we didn’t offer enough care.”

The objection, answered in the same tone  
“Autonomy.” Autonomy to refuse treatment already exists. Autonomy to demand the state end a non-terminal life is a different claim. It needs its own vote, not an amendment smuggled through a court case about people who were already dying.

“Suffering is suffering.” True. So is scarcity of housing, psychiatry, and palliative beds. A law that treats those as reasons for death will be used that way.

The punchline that is also the policy  
Mercy for the dying is a limited license. Mercy for everyone who is tired of living is a different regime. Write the second one honestly or don’t write it. Restore the first.

Iran says its naval forces have captured a U.S. REMUS 600 underwater drone in the Strait of Hormuz, with specialists examining the vehicle to recover its data. The U.S. military disputes the reported seizure.

In its September 27 announcement, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps identified the drone as the second American underwater vehicle it had seized. The IRGC Navy said intelligence and electronic warfare operations enabled the capture and accused the vehicle of conducting espionage.

IRGC spokesman Brigadier General Hossein Mohebi called it an “intelligence prize.” Identifying the equipment as a Mk 18 Mod 2 Kingfish, he portrayed the reported capture as evidence of Iran’s ability to intercept American underwater operations, according to Press TV.

Washington offered a competing account. CENTCOM spokesman Capt. Tim Hawkins said U.S. forces maintained “positive control of all of our operational drone assets,” in comments to Al Jazeera reported by Roya News.

The REMUS platform supports several military missions. Manufacturer HII says the REMUS 600M mine countermeasures variant uses sonar to survey underwater areas and locate potential mines. Intelligence collection is also among the broader REMUS family’s applications.

For Iran, the claimed intelligence gain depends on what specialists can retrieve. Press TV asserted access to encrypted data and navigation technology, but presented no recovered material demonstrating that access. The IRGC Navy’s statement described an effort to recover information without identifying what had been successfully extracted.

What Does 'The Prayers of the Righteous Availeth Much' Mean?
Doubt less and pray big. Worry less and pray often. Pray more for others than you do for yourself and you will see benefits as well. When you pray like this, your righteous prayers will avail much.
Jennifer Heeren
Published May 27, 2021

What Does 'The Prayers of the Righteous Availeth Much' Mean?
James 5:16 tells us to, “Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much” (KJV). The New King James Version simplifies the language a bit. It says, “Confess your trespasses to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The effective, fervent prayer of a righteous man avails much.”

Availeth, or to avail, means to use or take advantage of an opportunity. It could also mean when we choose to do good things in order to bring about good benefits.

More modern translations make it even clearer. The New International Version says, “Confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous person is powerful and effective.” The New Living Translation adds that “the earnest prayer of a righteous person has great power and produces wonderful results.” This goes along with the avail definition of doing good things to bring about good benefits. Then the Amplified Bible translation states, “the heartfelt and persistent prayer of a righteous man can accomplish much when put into action and made effective by God. It has tremendous power.”

What Does 'The Prayers of the Righteous Availeth Much' Mean?
We need to confess our sins to God and to other people. Confession will heal many souls. The one that confesses and the one that hears will both experience healing because confession brings God’s redemption into the picture. The confessor feels relief and the listener feels hope because they know they will sin too. Redemption brings much hope. Our conscience is cleared, and our prayers will be heard by God.

The eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer (1 Peter 3:12). When we choose to do good and godly things, we are in the perfect place for God to hear our prayers. When we repent and confess our sins, God will turn his ears toward our cries (Psalm 34:15). He longs to help us when we humbly admit our weaknesses.

James follows verse 16 with a description of Elijah. Elijah was merely a human, just like us, but he let his faith in God prevail by praying fervently. He prayed that it wouldn’t rain, and it didn’t rain for three years and six months. Then he prayed again for it to rain and heaven poured forth rain. When we put our faith in God, our prayers can do more than we think or imagine.

We can pray bigger than we think we can. Jesus said that if we have faith and do not doubt, we can move a mountain (Matthew 21:21). Whether He meant this literally or figuratively, we know that He meant for us to pray for big, even impossible, things. With God, impossible things are made possible. We can do great things because the Holy Spirit is within us. Our prayers avail much when we push aside our doubts and pray big.

3 Ways We Can Apply This Verse to Our Lives Today
The Book of James is a very practical book. It is often thought of as the Proverbs of the New Testament. James 5:16 can lead us into dramatic living within God’s purposes when we remember these 3 things:

1. We need community. Relationships with other people are very important for righteous living. When we do wrong, we should admit it to other people. We shouldn’t try to hide our flaws. We show our humanness and therefore make it possible for others to relate to us. We are transparent with them and therefore bring about an atmosphere where they can be completely honest with us. We play a part in the healing of other people around us. At least we can if we take the opportunity. We can help people heal physically, mentally, and spiritually.

Use your gifts and your prayers to serve and encourage others. Teach them. Give generously to them. Lead them in the right direction. Be kind and open to hearing the troubles they may be going through. You won’t always have an answer for them, but you can point them to the One who does. Prayers avail much when we use them to figure out the best way to serve others and then we go out and serve them.

2. We should ask for and give prayer. When we feel weak, we ask other people to pray for us. We ask for encouraging advice. We ask for help when we are burdened and weighed down. Then, we also offer to pray for others. We come beside them when they seem tired and lack joy. We speak encouraging words to them. We pray encouragement over them. We lift them up to our Heavenly Father so He can carry the bulk of their burden.

Keep your prayers as simple as possible. Flowery, long-winded phrases are unnecessary. Words like that are usually said to impress other people. God isn’t impressed by how we say things. He’s impressed by our humble heart. And He knows our needs before we say them. Prayers avail much when we say them out of a humble heart that desperately wants to help others.

3. We turn these actions into everyday habits. We continually give prayer the opportunity to lift up others as well as ourselves. Any good that we accomplish is because of God’s grace. He is the one who gave us the motivation to do any good works at all. We try our best to help others but then let God fill in the inevitable mistakes that we make. He can take them a lot further than our advice can. We pray for them to be open to the Lord’s leading and the same for ourselves. Our help can avail much but God can bring about even more power as well as deliverance, restoration, and redemption.

Prayers avail much when they help point people to the God who created them, loves them, and longs to be in a relationship with them.

Praying in a Way that “Availeth Much”
It is key to remember that if we confess our sins to God and to one another, God is faithful and just to forgive us and purify us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9). Then we can be confident that God hears us when we pray for things that please Him (1 John 5:14). When we ask, we will receive from God if our motivations are to keep His commandments and do what pleases Him (1 John 3:22).

Pray that God will shed light onto people’s hearts so that they will be convicted of their wrong actions and thinking. Pray for harmony and peace so that arguments will be doused with God’s living water. Pray that plots of evil and revenge are thwarted. Your prayers can play a part in turning someone toward God.

Doubt less and pray big. Worry less and pray often. Pray more for others than you do for yourself and you will see benefits as well. When you pray like this, your righteous prayers will avail much.

The Cherokee called her the War Woman. She was a tall, red-haired, cross-eyed frontier wife who could not read or write, and according to the most famous story of the Georgia backcountry, she once captured a whole squad of enemy soldiers single-handedly, in her own cabin, with their own guns. Her name was Nancy Hart, and she is the only woman in the history of Georgia to have a county named after her.

Hart lived on the raw Georgia frontier during the Revolution, in a region torn apart by a savage, personal civil war between Patriots and Loyalists. She was a fierce rebel, and she made no secret of it. She spied, she smuggled, and she was known to disguise herself to gather information on the enemy. The Loyalists and their Native allies knew her and feared her temper, and she earned that ominous nickname, the War Woman, with a creek near her home named for her.

The legend that made her immortal goes like this. A group of Loyalist soldiers, five or six of them, came to her isolated cabin one day. They had been hunting a Patriot leader, and they barged in, bragging about their deeds, and demanded that Nancy cook for them. She played the part of the grumbling but obliging hostess. She killed the last turkey, set it cooking, and, crucially, kept the men's cups full of wine and corn liquor. As the soldiers relaxed, ate, drank, and let their guard down, they stacked their muskets against the wall, out of easy reach.

That was their mistake. There was a gap or chink in the cabin's log wall, and as the men grew drunk and careless, Nancy quietly began slipping their muskets, one at a time, out through that opening to the outside, while sending her daughter to signal for help. She got several guns out before the soldiers noticed. When one of them finally realized what was happening and lunged for the weapons, Nancy snatched up a musket, leveled it, and warned them she would shoot any man who moved. One did. She shot him dead. Another rushed her, and she shot him too. Then she held the rest at gunpoint, alone, until her husband and neighbors arrived.

And the ending is grim frontier justice. The surviving Loyalists begged to be treated as prisoners of war. Nancy would have none of it. She insisted, over milder suggestions, that shooting was too good for them, and the captured Tories were hanged.

For a long time this was dismissed by some as pure tall tale, backcountry folklore that grew with the telling, and to be fair, the details have surely been polished over two centuries. But then history offered a chilling footnote. Generations later, in the early 1900s, workers building a railroad near the site of Hart's old cabin dug up a neat row of skeletons in a shallow grave, right where the story said the bodies should be. Bones do not prove every detail of a legend. But they gave the story a weight that has never quite gone away.

Georgia never forgot her. They named a county after her, Hart County, the only one in the entire state named for a woman, along with a lake and a town. Remember Nancy Hart, the War Woman, who did not wait for an army to protect her home, and who proved that on the Revolutionary frontier, some of the most dangerous soldiers around were not soldiers at all.

They told you Donald Trump was a Russian asset. 

They told you he was a Nazi. 

They told you, for years, in every major media outlet in America, that the man was an existential threat to democracy itself.

Once you've told a country that, you have justified nearly anything.

So the apparatus went to work. Surveillance warrants on a campaign. A dossier funded by his opponent, laundered into intelligence channels. A special counsel, years of it, and a collusion case that never materialized. Note the sequence. The threat justified the measures. The threat turned out to be fake but the measures stayed.

Now he's back as president, and this time he came prepared. The corrupt agencies are being cleaned out. The pathway that they used last time has been closed.

So here is the question the Canadian press gallery will not ask. When the people are willing to do that to their own president lose the ability to do it from the inside, do they simply stop? Or do they find a new position outside his reach?

Because there is an obvious one. A G7 country. With the longest undefended border on earth. Buried deep in his supply chains. Holding a veto over the industrial states that decide elections. And are entirely beyond the jurisdiction of every agency he just took back.

Why capture an agency when you can capture a country?

But a country is not an agency. You cannot subpoena it or leak to it. To turn one against him you would need the right man at the top, and the specification is brutally narrow.

He could not be bought. A bought man leaves a trail.

You would need the perfect Manchurian candidate. Not a man who knows what he is. A man so thoroughly conditioned by a lifetime inside the old order that he cannot see it. No handler. No instruction. Ask him and he would deny it sincerely, because to him it was never betrayal. It was maturity. The adult position. Sacrificing the smaller thing for the greater good, and never once noticing that the smaller thing was his own country.

He would need to be formed in the institutions that built that order. Central banking. Global finance. The summit circuit. A career teaching him that the nation state is an administrative unit and that real authority sits above it.

He would need to be a technician. Someone who can move a state without appearing to move it.

He would need standing on both sides of the border, so that divided loyalty reads as a résumé.

And he would need to arrive clean. No riding to nurse. No faction that made him. No debts to anyone in the party he was about to lead, and therefore no one inside it with the standing to stop him. Not a politician. An operator.

That man is almost impossible to find.

And yet Canada made him Prime Minister in March.

He took over the Liberal leadership at the worst possible moment for anyone who actually wanted a political career. He captured a radioactive brand at the worst time in its political cycle. He jumped anyway. When a man accepts a terrible deal, you should stop asking what it cost him and start asking what he was seeking to gain.

Three days before he announced, he was not in Edmonton. He was on American television, in full campaign register, aimed at the wrong country. Why would a Canadian soft launch their Canadian political career on an American television show?

Then the pattern fills in. He creates a Chief Operating Officer of the Prime Minister's Office, a position that has never existed in the history of this country, and fills it with a former Hillary Clinton American Democratic operative. The same Hillary Clinton whose campaign paid for the dossier. The one that laundered a foreign spy's gossip into an instrument of the American state. Carney closes a Washington-cohosted summit in Toronto with the Canadian press kept outside the room. His portfolio is ninety-one percent American.

And in August, the trade talks collapsed.

Here is where an honest writer stops and tells you what he does not know. Nobody outside that room knows what Washington actually demanded. It’s never been publicly released. Carney says the Americans asked too much and offered too little. Washington says that is false. Two accounts that are clearly contradictory, and there is no transcript. We are in the fog of war, and we will stay there until the documents surface a decade from now, if they ever do. What we can look at is the convenience of the timing.

But lets set aside the disputed part and look only at what nobody denies.

Carney suspended the talks. Carney recalled the negotiators. And when the retaliation came, Canada did not simply mirror the American tariffs. It selected. Over seven hundred products, and the pain was directed at Ohio, Pennsylvania, Michigan and Wisconsin, weeks before the midterm elections.

What do we call a foreign government inflicting targeted economic pain on specific electorates immediately before an election? In any other decade we had a phrase for that.
And what did Canada get?

Elbows up. That was the war cry. So where are the spoils of war? Where is the reindustrialization of Canada’s industrial base? Where is the diversified market access that was supposed to free us from the Americans? Where is the pipelines to tidewater, the expanded ports, the LNG plants? Groceries are not cheaper. Rent is not cheaper. The tariffs still sit on our backs. A full year of the loudest confrontation with our largest trading partner in living memory has bought this country nothing you can point to, photograph, or carry home.

Look closer, though, and we will find that the benefits of the last year do exist, its just that they have accrued in someone else's name.

Every dollar of that confrontation flowed one way. The rhetoric ran north, warm and patriotic, elbows up for the cameras. The structure ran south. A Prime Minister whose portfolio is overwhelmingly American, whose closest operator is an American Democratic strategist, whose summits are convened by Washington, spent a year manufacturing a crisis whose targeted casualties landed in precisely the American swing states that decide who governs from that same city. We paid the tariffs. His faction across the border collected the political dividend. Ask who this actually served and the flag on the podium stops matching the balance sheet behind it.

Set every fact down on its own and each one has an innocent face. The portfolio is just a retirement account from a long career. The progressive American political operator is just a hire. The timing is just the calendar. The targeting of the swing states with tariffs are just how trade math works. That is exactly why it holds. A single coincidence is invisible. It is only when you lay them end to end, all of them pointing the same direction, all of them costing Canada and paying his American allies.

The ambition was never to be our Prime Minister. The office was the means. A credential that let him capture Canada and turn it into a forward operating base, a country pointed south and spent against Donald Trump in an American civil war that has cost the Canadian people dearly and bought them nothing.
You have to ask the question eventually. How many coincidences, at this altitude, in this direction, before you stop calling them coincidences?

He is not governing this country. He is occupying it.

Stop thinking of the United States as a foreign country and start thinking of it as what it actually is, a global American empire that governs through markets, currency, media and defence rather than through legions, and whose provinces keep their own flags and anthems as a courtesy. On that map Canada is not a neighbour. We are the richest province in the system, wired directly into the metropole.

So when Caesar took Rome, Pompey did not surrender. He crossed to Greece and kept the war going from the provinces, because a faction that loses the capital does not stop fighting. It relocates. They lost Washington. They went to the most valuable province they had, the one that was already theirs, and they garrisoned it with a man of their own class who needed no persuading at all. He did not have to be recruited. He was already one of them, and the province came with the office.

Which is why the whole performance has been aimed south. The elbows, the flags, the defiance. It was never Canadian politics. It was American theatre, staged here, for them.
Canada is not being governed. It is being occupied, a province held by the losing faction in the global American empire's civil war.

text:
Four Scarcities Reshaping Agent Infrastructure Economics

Meta($META ) launched Muse on September 8, a personal AI agent capable of executing tasks autonomously in the background, powered by Muse Spark, Meta's first frontier model that no longer publishes algorithm parameters. Within 12 days, US mobile daily active users reached 642,000, exceeding ChatGPT's 231,000 at the equivalent launch point, and Muse topped both the App Store and Google Play. At Meta Connect on September 23, Zuckerberg outlined the monetization structure: a $20/month Power plan and a $100/month Maximum plan.

These figures invite a growth narrative. But Muse exposes a more fundamental problem: when AI migrates from conversational interaction to autonomous execution, the scarcity structure of infrastructure rearranges. The market currently estimates agent infrastructure demand with a linear model — DAU multiplied by per-user compute — that fails systematically when applied to products like Muse. Not because compute stops mattering, but because no single compute bottleneck determines infrastructure scale. Four interdependent scarcities do, each with a different mitigation path, time constant, and cost elasticity.

From token pricing to cost per completed task.

The unit economics of an agent cannot be read from token prices. Meta's Muse Spark 1.3 pricing is $1.25 per million input tokens, $4.25 per million output tokens, and $0.15 per million cached input tokens. The Contributor tier — where data is used for training — prices input at $0.10, output at $0.20, and cached input at $0.002. Artificial Analysis estimates Muse Spark 1.3 at approximately $0.55 per task on the Intelligence Index. On the surface, competitive pricing.

But the cost per API call is not the cost per task. An agent task involves tool loops, retries, cache misses, and multi-step reasoning. When an edit succeeds after two failed attempts, total attempts equal three. Cache misses force context re-reads. Browser execution and search calls settle outside Meta's billing system. Research on Cost per Completed Task (CPCT) as a measurement framework shows that token price is a weak proxy for agentic workload economics: in a measured case study, capping tool-output verbosity reduced the cost of an identical task by 88%, an 8.6x swing attributable entirely to operational overhead, not model capability. The economic unit is the accepted work, not the token.

For infrastructure planning, this means Muse's inference demand is driven by the distribution of task complexity multiplied by task volume, not by user count multiplied by fixed token consumption. A user submitting one "research competitor pricing strategy" request may generate 50 to 100 model invocations across search, data extraction, long-context synthesis, and multi-turn validation. A user submitting 20 simple queries may generate fewer than half that. The variance in task complexity distribution, not the arithmetic mean of user count, drives infrastructure demand.

Microsoft's study published in Joule in April 2026 provides the energy distribution baseline. For a typical query (about 300 output tokens), median energy is 0.31 Wh. When response length rises to about 5,000 tokens — long code generation or multi-step reasoning — median energy jumps to 3.91 Wh, roughly 13 times the typical query. More critically, Microsoft found that "a relatively small proportion of expensive requests can dominate total electricity consumption." In a scale projection of 1 billion requests per day, if 10% shift to long-reasoning tasks, electricity demand rises from 0.7 GWh to 1.7 GWh, and even after optimization requires 0.8 GWh. A 10-percentage-point shift in request mix more than doubles total energy consumption.

Layered on Muse's architecture: safety classifiers, routing decisions, and tool-selection steps represent the majority of backend invocations, but if 10% to 20% involve complex planning or multi-turn reasoning, overall energy consumption deviates significantly from what the median suggests. The proportion is unknown at Muse's current stage, but its impact on infrastructure cost is non-linear.

Memory: the server-count determinant that replaces CPU.

In conventional data center planning, server count is set by compute demand, with memory and storage as proportional attachments. In agent inference, this logic inverts.

DeepSeek's DSec sandbox platform, published in September 2026, offers the highest-density production data available: a single production unit of about 160 CPU nodes, 30,000 physical cores, and 250 TB memory, with peak concurrency exceeding 380,000 sandboxes. A single node hosts up to 800 microVMs. But this density rests on two strict conditions: about 90% of instances average no more than 5% of requested CPU, and the platform uses aggressive memory overcommitment — through virtio-pmem with DAX, microVMs skip their own page cache and map host physical memory directly, reducing peak memory consumption by 40.2%.

Muse's persistent environment differs fundamentally from DSec's training sandbox. Training sandboxes are ephemeral. Muse's per-user environment carries browser activity, credential management, database I/O, and long-lived state. Research on agentic browser workloads shows that median sandbox peak DRAM usage is about 0.8 GB, but per-session peak can reach 28 GB during compilation and unit tests. For a 32K-context agent session with a 70B-class model using Grouped Query Attention, the KV cache alone consumes 2 to 12 GB of GPU memory per request depending on model architecture.

Muse's published architecture assigns each environment about 2 vCPUs, 8 GB RAM, and 100 GB storage. Observed memory usage for a single environment was about 3 GB. But including platform overhead, physical memory residency has a floor around 6 GB. An application server with 3 TB memory hosts about 500 active environments at 6 GB each — not the larger number calculated from CPU core count. This means server count may be determined by memory bandwidth and capacity, not compute core count. Raising CPU oversubscription ratios alone will not reduce server count, because memory is the binding constraint.

The supply constraint on memory is tighter than on CPUs. HBM4 per-GB cost has jumped from $17 to $18 in the HBM3E era to $31 to $32, with Bernstein projecting further rises to $53 per GB by 2027. UBS estimates HBM average pricing will rise about 79% in 2027 versus 2026. HBM production consumes approximately 3x the wafer capacity of standard DDR5, with yields in the 55% range versus DDR5's 90%+. The three major manufacturers' HBM capacity has exceeded 355,000 wafers per month, rising from 8% of global DRAM wafer starts two years ago to 23% today. For agent platforms, every additional active user environment increases memory demand in two directions simultaneously: application server DDR5 and accelerator-side HBM.

Storage: the quantity that dwarfs compute in absolute volume.

Agent persistent environments are not only a compute problem. Each user environment must persist file systems, application data, history, and context. Muse assigns 100 GB storage per environment. If 100 million DAU corresponds to 75 million to 100 million retained accounts, at 50% utilization, total storage demand reaches 3.75 EB to 5 EB. This exceeds a substantial proportion of current global data center storage.

The storage constraint has a different structure from memory. Marginal cost per TB is far lower — as of August 2026, a 30 TB TLC enterprise SSD costs approximately $22,600, while an equivalent HDD costs approximately $1,216, putting flash at 18.6x the price of disk per terabyte. HDD prices themselves have risen from $495 in Q3 2025 to $1,216, a 2.5x increase. Seagate and Western Digital have both told investors nearline HDD output is sold out through 2027. A neocloud without a hyperscaler-scale supply agreement is buying at spot prices, which carry a 30% to 40% premium.

This means storage cost optimization depends on tiering efficiency, not on unit cost reduction. DeepSeek's tiered loading strategy in DSec provides a reference: through versioned image layers and on-demand loading, an 8,192-container burst completed startup in about 35 minutes with 57% less disk-write traffic. If agent platforms cannot achieve comparable tiering efficiency, storage becomes a larger-than-expected cost line — not because per-TB prices are high, but because the absolute volume at 1 billion DAU approaches 50 EB at 50% utilization of the 100 GB quota.

Network topology: the constraint that scales with geography.

Muse's architecture requires each user's agent environment to maintain controlled connections with inference infrastructure. When users are geographically dispersed, data residency requirements apply, and latency-sensitive tasks demand edge inference, network topology complexity rises. The industry has converged on a three-tier framework: scale-up (within a rack, typically copper, a few meters), scale-out (across racks within a data center, direct-detect pluggable optics, hundreds of meters to a few kilometers), and scale-across (across data center facilities, coherent optics, tens to hundreds of kilometers).

For agent workloads, all three tiers carry traffic simultaneously. A user in Singapore interacting with an agent hosted in Virginia triggers scale-across traffic on every tool call. An 800G optical transceiver consumes 13 to 16 watts per port. At 100 million DAU with even modest cross-region traffic, the aggregate port count and power draw from optical interconnects becomes a material infrastructure cost that is structurally distinct from compute and memory.

CPO and silicon photonics are the technology paths to reducing this cost. Nvidia's $4 billion in strategic investments in Lumentum and Coherent during 2026, and Ciena's hyper-rail photonics platform targeting 128-fiber-pair density, indicate the industry expects optical interconnect to scale. But the capacity constraint is binding: Lumentum and Coherent together hold roughly 40% of the high-power laser supply critical to CPO deployment, and their combined 2026 capacity is already largely booked. CPO port shipments are projected at 120,000 units in 2026, concentrated in North American and East Asian top-tier compute clusters — insufficient for the agent inference wave. This constraint has a supply-side time constant of 18 to 24 months for laser capacity expansion, longer than memory or storage.

The capital markets gap.

Meta's 2027 capital expenditure has been revised upward by both Citi and Morgan Stanley. Citi estimates $205 billion, raised approximately 22%, tied to Meta's target of about 14 GW compute capacity. Morgan Stanley forecasts $225 billion for 2027 and $250 billion for 2028, up from $145 billion in 2025. Citi warns that all three major hyperscalers will enter negative free cash flow territory in both 2027 and 2028.

Comparing this capex scale against Muse's economics yields an informative judgment. If 15% to 25% of Meta's 2027 capex — $31 billion to $51 billion — is allocated to Muse and related inference infrastructure, the corresponding compute capacity supports tens of millions to hundreds of millions of DAU under reasonable efficiency assumptions. But Meta's capex simultaneously serves AI features across Instagram, Facebook, WhatsApp, and other platforms, with Muse being one allocation among many. The fixed capex commitment is made against a variable DAU conversion, and the mismatch between the two is where the risk sits — not in the capex number itself.

On the revenue side, Muse's $20 and $100 monthly pricing points imply that at 100 million DAU with 10% paid conversion, split 80/20 between the two tiers, annual revenue is approximately $4.3 billion. The ratio between this revenue and the estimated infrastructure cost requires careful evaluation, particularly given that the task complexity distribution — and therefore the per-user infrastructure cost — is not yet observable.

For semiconductor investors, the implication is that no single "DAU to accelerator" conversion coefficient can underwrite revenue forecasts for NVIDIA, Micron, SanDisk, or optical component suppliers. The four scarcities — energy distribution, memory density, storage volume, and optical network capacity — should be modeled separately, each cross-analyzed against its respective supply constraint. A bottleneck in any one dimension changes the deployment cadence and cost structure for all four. The scarcity that binds first determines the infrastructure buildout pace; the scarcity that binds longest determines the total cost.
